title: Brent, WTI and an unrelated price: levels, returns, fat tails and changing volatility

explain.prompt: The trader says: “Brent and WTI have a correlation of 0.996 — they're basically the same thing. And coffee is at 0.82, funny.” In 4–6 sentences with your numbers: what level correlations and return correlations each tell you, what the distribution and volatility of Brent returns look like, and what the spread table already suggests.
rubric: Level correlations measure shared trends: Brent–WTI 0.996, but WTI–coffee 0.82 for two unrelated markets. A high correlation of levels is not evidence of a relationship.
Daily log returns answer a different question — do the prices move together day by day? Brent–WTI 0.82 (Pearson) / 0.80 (Spearman); WTI–coffee 0.006: coffee's 0.82 was only two trends.
Pearson and Spearman are close for Brent–WTI returns: no handful of days drives the co-movement; Spearman is the safer check with fat tails.

Brent returns: mean −0.023 %, median −0.014 %, std 1.77 % a day, excess kurtosis 0.98 — moderately fat tails. Volatility is not constant: 60-day annualised volatility ranges from 15 % (late 2012) to 48 % (September 2014); 19 % in 2012 vs 38 % in 2015.

The Brent–WTI spread averages 19.7 $/bbl in 2012 and 21.4 in 2013, then about 1.5–4 from 2016 on: the relationship between the two levels changed — something to test before assuming one stable equilibrium (4.4).
